name: Event-Driven E-Commerce Processing
description: Design an event-driven architecture on AWS for an e-commerce order processing system with decoupled services, fanout processing, and workflow orchestration.
user_problem: Design an event-driven architecture on AWS for an e-commerce order processing system with the following requirements: (1) Decoupled services that communicate via events for order placement, payment processing, inventory management, and shipping, (2) An event bus for routing events between producers and consumers with filtering rules, (3) Fanout and parallel processing of events to multiple downstream services, (4) Workflow orchestration for multi-step order fulfillment processes, (5) Serverless compute for event processing with automatic scaling, (6) Reliable message delivery with dead-letter queues for failed processing, (7) Real-time notifications to customers on order status changes, (8) Monitoring, tracing, and auditing of all event flows.

reference_architecture.full_text:
An event-driven architecture uses events to trigger and communicate between decoupled services and is common in modern applications built with microservices. An event is a change in state or an update, like an item being placed in a shopping cart on an e-commerce website or an order being shipped. Events can either carry the state (the item purchased, its price, and a delivery address) or events can be identifiers (a notification that an order was shipped). Event-driven architectures have three key components: event producers, event routers, and event consumers. A producer publishes an event to the router, which filters and pushes the events to consumers. Producer services and consumer services are decoupled, which allows them to be scaled, updated, and deployed independently. Two common options when building applications are request-response and event-driven architecture. In request-response architecture, an application's components communicate via synchronous API calls with tight coupling. In event-driven architecture, the client generates an event and can immediately move on to its next task, while different parts of the application respond to the event as needed.

Challenges Solved by Event-Driven Architecture: In a typical ecommerce application that uses a synchronous API, the client makes a request to place an order and the order service sends the request downstream to an invoice service. As more services are added (fulfillment, forecasting, shipping, rewards), the order service accumulates more responsibilities and more complexity. The order service must know how to call each service's API, from the call structure to the retry semantics. If there are backwards-incompatible changes to the APIs, the order service team must update them. The system forwards heavy traffic spikes to dependencies, which may not have the same scaling capabilities. Dependent services may transmit errors back up the stack to the client. Error handling becomes extremely complex: if fulfillment fails because products are out of stock, the system must alert the invoice service, reverse the payment or issue a refund, update forecasting, and handle shipping service failures. Coordinating these remediation workflows across all unhappy paths in an API-driven application becomes increasingly difficult. Event-driven architectures solve these challenges through decoupling.

Event Bus and Routing Layer: Amazon EventBridge serves as the central serverless event bus that routes events between services. EventBridge uses a predefined schema for events and allows you to create rules that are applied across the entire event body to filter before pushing to consumers. EventBridge is recommended when building applications that react to events from SaaS applications, AWS services, or custom applications. EventBridge supports over 100 built-in event sources and can receive custom events from application services. EventBridge Schema Registry automatically discovers and stores event schemas, generating code bindings in Java, Python, and TypeScript for type-safe event handling. EventBridge Pipes connect event sources to targets with optional filtering, enrichment, and transformation steps. EventBridge rules support content-based filtering on any field in the event JSON payload, including nested fields, arrays, and numeric ranges. Multiple rules can match the same event, enabling fanout to multiple targets simultaneously. EventBridge archives events for replay, enabling recovery from processing failures by replaying historical events. EventBridge has built-in retry policies with configurable maximum retry attempts and maximum event age, and dead-letter queues for events that cannot be delivered.

Fanout and Messaging Layer: Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) enables high-throughput, low-latency fanout from a single event to thousands or millions of endpoints. SNS supports both application-to-application (A2A) communication for distributing events to SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/HTTPS endpoints, and Kinesis Data Firehose, and application-to-person (A2P) communication for customer notifications via email, SMS, and mobile push notifications. SNS message filtering allows subscribers to receive only a subset of messages based on filter policies. In the e-commerce context, when an order is placed, SNS fans out the order event simultaneously to the payment processing queue, inventory management queue, analytics pipeline, and customer notification endpoints. SNS FIFO topics provide strict ordering and exactly-once delivery when paired with SQS FIFO queues. Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) provides reliable message queuing to decouple services, absorbing traffic spikes and ensuring reliable delivery. SQS supports standard queues for maximum throughput with at-least-once delivery, and FIFO queues for exactly-once processing with strict ordering. SQS visibility timeout prevents multiple consumers from processing the same message simultaneously. SQS dead-letter queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail processing after a configurable number of retry attempts, preventing data loss and enabling investigation of persistent failures. Dead-letter queue redrive allows reprocessing of failed messages after the underlying issue is resolved. SQS Extended Client Library supports messages up to 2 GB using S3 for large payloads like order documents. SQS long polling reduces empty responses and costs.

Serverless Compute Layer: AWS Lambda provides serverless compute for processing events with automatic scaling and built-in high availability. Lambda runs code in response to events without provisioning or managing servers, supporting Node.js, Python, Java, Go, .NET, Ruby, and custom runtimes. Lambda automatically scales from zero to thousands of concurrent executions based on the number of incoming events. Lambda supports reserved concurrency to guarantee capacity for critical functions (such as payment processing) and provisioned concurrency to eliminate cold start latency for latency-sensitive operations. Each Lambda function has a dedicated IAM execution role with least-privilege permissions. Lambda Destinations route successful or failed asynchronous invocation results to downstream services like SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or another Lambda function, simplifying error handling without custom code. Lambda event source mappings integrate with SQS, enabling automatic polling and batch processing of queued messages. Lambda Layers share common code and dependencies across functions. Lambda functions can be configured with VPC access for connecting to private resources like RDS databases.

Workflow Orchestration Layer: AWS Step Functions orchestrates multi-step order fulfillment workflows, coordinating Lambda functions and other AWS services in a visual, JSON-defined state machine. Step Functions Standard Workflows support long-running processes (up to one year) with exactly-once execution, while Express Workflows handle high-volume, short-duration tasks (up to five minutes) with at-least-once execution. Step Functions provides built-in error handling with Retry blocks (configurable backoff and max attempts), Catch blocks (routing to fallback states), and Timeout states. Parallel states execute multiple branches simultaneously—for example, processing payment, updating inventory, and generating an invoice in parallel after order validation. Choice states implement conditional routing logic based on order attributes, payment status, or inventory availability. Wait states pause execution for a specified time or until a specific timestamp, useful for payment settlement periods. Map states iterate over collections, processing each order line item independently. Step Functions integrates directly with over 200 AWS services including DynamoDB (read/write items), SQS (send messages), SNS (publish notifications), ECS (run tasks), and API Gateway (invoke APIs) using optimized service integrations that eliminate the need for Lambda functions as intermediaries. In the e-commerce context, a typical order fulfillment workflow proceeds as follows: (1) Validate Order state checks order data integrity, (2) Parallel state simultaneously processes payment via a Lambda function calling a payment processor, reserves inventory via DynamoDB conditional writes, and creates an invoice record, (3) Choice state evaluates payment and inventory results and routes to success or failure paths, (4) on success, a Fulfill Order state triggers warehouse operations, (5) Ship Order state integrates with the shipping provider and generates tracking information, (6) Notify Customer state publishes order confirmation and shipping details via SNS.

API and Frontend Integration Layer: Amazon API Gateway provides REST APIs for the e-commerce frontend to place orders, check order status, manage user profiles, and browse products. API Gateway integrates with Lambda functions for request processing and can also integrate directly with EventBridge to publish events from API calls without a Lambda intermediary. API Gateway supports request validation, request/response transformation, throttling (to protect backend services from traffic spikes during flash sales), and API keys with usage plans. API Gateway stages (dev, staging, prod) and canary deployments enable safe rollout of API changes. API Gateway caching reduces backend load for frequently accessed data like product catalogs.

Data Storage Layer: Amazon DynamoDB stores order data, inventory counts, customer information, and shopping cart state as a fast, flexible serverless NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale. DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode automatically adapts to traffic patterns, handling sudden spikes during flash sales without capacity planning. DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes in real-time, triggering Lambda functions for event propagation when orders change status. DynamoDB transactions provide ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable) operations for critical business logic like transferring inventory from available to reserved status during order placement. DynamoDB Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) enable efficient queries by order status, customer ID, date range, and other access patterns. DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) provides continuous backups. Amazon S3 stores order documents (invoices, receipts, shipping labels), product images, catalog data, and static frontend assets. S3 event notifications can trigger Lambda functions when new documents are uploaded. S3 lifecycle policies archive old order documents to S3 Glacier for cost-effective long-term retention.

Authentication Layer: Amazon Cognito provides user authentication and authorization for customers interacting with the e-commerce frontend. Cognito User Pools manage user registration, sign-in, and account recovery. Cognito Identity Pools provide temporary AWS credentials for authenticated users to access AWS resources directly (such as uploading images to S3). Cognito integrates with API Gateway as a JWT authorizer, validating access tokens on every API request. Cognito supports social identity federation (Google, Facebook, Amazon) and enterprise identity providers via SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

Observability Layer: Amazon CloudWatch monitors all services and provides unified dashboards and alarms for operational visibility. CloudWatch Metrics tracks Lambda invocations, error rates, duration, and throttles; SQS queue depth and age of oldest message; DynamoDB read/write capacity utilization; API Gateway request count and latency. CloudWatch Logs aggregates logs from Lambda functions, API Gateway, and Step Functions execution history. CloudWatch Alarms trigger notifications via SNS when operational thresholds are breached, such as elevated order failure rates, growing DLQ depth, or increased API latency. AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing to track requests across services and identify bottlenecks. X-Ray traces follow an order from API Gateway through Lambda, EventBridge, SQS, Step Functions, and DynamoDB, providing a complete view of the order processing pipeline. X-Ray service maps visualize the topology of all e-commerce microservices and their dependencies. AWS CloudTrail enables audit logging for all API calls across the architecture, recording who performed what action, when, and from where—essential for PCI-DSS compliance in payment processing.

The end-to-end order processing flow is as follows: (1) A customer authenticates via Cognito and places an order through the REST API hosted on API Gateway. (2) API Gateway validates the request and invokes a Lambda function that writes the order to DynamoDB and publishes an 'OrderPlaced' event to EventBridge. (3) EventBridge evaluates rules and routes the event to multiple targets: an SNS topic for fanout, an SQS queue for payment processing, and a Step Functions state machine for order fulfillment orchestration. (4) The SNS topic fans out the event to the inventory service (SQS queue), analytics pipeline (Lambda), and customer notification service (email/SMS). (5) The Step Functions state machine orchestrates the fulfillment workflow: validates the order, processes payment, reserves inventory, generates the invoice, coordinates fulfillment, triggers shipping, and notifies the customer at each stage. (6) If any step fails, Step Functions retry logic handles transient errors. Persistent failures route messages to SQS dead-letter queues and trigger CloudWatch Alarms for operator intervention. (7) The customer receives real-time order status updates via SNS notifications. (8) All interactions are traced by X-Ray, logged in CloudWatch, and audited by CloudTrail.
